children: By Dow Jones Newswires staff
Below are the most important global events likely to affect FX and bond markets in the week starting Nov. 16.

The minutes of the Federal Reserve's October meeting will be among the key areas of focus in the week ahead as markets search for clues on the timing and extent of further possible interest-rate rises.
Market expectations for another Fed rate rise in December have increased in the wake of stronger-than-expected jobs data and higher-than-anticipated inflation.
U.K. data will also be closely monitored to gauge whether elevated rate-rise expectations for the Bank of England are justified.

In Asia, Japan's growth and inflation figures and China's monthly activity data will offer fresh readings on the region's biggest economies, as leaders gather in Shenzhen for the APEC summit. Bank Indonesia's interest-rate decision will also be in focus as policymakers balance support for growth with pressure to keep the rupiah stable.
U.S.
The Federal Reserve will release the minutes of its October meeting on Wednesday.
The Fed held interest rates steady in October even after data showed inflation accelerated in September.
"A question is whether the Fed regrets holding rates steady at its meeting last month and wants to play 'catch-up'," Investec Economics analysts said in a note.

Since the meeting, rate-rise prospects have been boosted by robust October jobs data, higher-than-expected inflation and Fed Governor Christopher Waller signaling the prospect of raising rates as much as 50 basis points in December.
The market prices an 89% chance of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December and an 11% chance of a 50 basis points move, LSEG data showed.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is also due to speak at the Fed's Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference on Monday.
In economic data, the Empire State Manufacturing Survey for November is due on Monday, followed by October retail sales on Tuesday.

October housing starts and pending home sales are due on Wednesday, while the weekly initial jobless claims and the November Philadelphia Fed Business Outlook Survey are due to be released on Thursday.
The final November University of Michigan consumer confidence survey is due on Friday.
Canada

Canada's October inflation data on Monday will be monitored for hints on whether the Bank of Canada could raise interest rates further. The BOC increased rates by 25 basis points to 2.5% last month based on a sharply higher outlook for inflation. Policymakers expect inflation to remain above 3% until late 2027 before slowing gradually to 2% by mid-2028. Annual inflation rose to 3.1% in September from 3% in August.
U.K.

The U.K. has a busy week ahead with key data releases. Attention will be on the jobs data due on Tuesday and the inflation on Wednesday, which could offer clues on the pace of interest-rate rises by the Bank of England. Investors have raised their expectations of more BOE rate increases in 2027 after the latest U.K. GDP data for September came in stronger than expected. Markets currently price in an 82% chance of a BOE rate increase in December, up from 50% probability last week, according to LSEG data.

Other data include the public-sector finance data for October due on Friday. It will be the first public finance data release since the U.K. Treasury chief John Healey delivered a relatively modest budget in October.
The U.K. retail sales data are also due to be released on Friday. The data could indicate whether or not high energy costs are hurting consumer spending.
Eurozone
The eurozone economic calendar is relatively quiet.
Eurozone industrial production data for September will be released on Monday, while the ZEW German economic sentiment survey for November is due on Tuesday.

The final reading of eurozone October inflation will be released Wednesday followed by September eurozone construction output data and balance of payments figures Thursday. The European Commission will publish its flash eurozone consumer confidence survey for November on Friday.
Hungary

The National Bank of Hungary announces its policy decision on Tuesday. The central bank is likely to keep interest rates on hold again at 5.50% after leaving rates steady in October as there haven't been enough changes since the last meeting to think this time will be different, ING analysts said in a note. Hungary's inflation remains subdued, the economy is nowhere near overheating, and the forint remains relatively stable, they said.
"Local factors create room for the NBH to lower rates, but we still don't expect any moves in the coming quarters because external risks remain elevated."
South Africa

South Africa's central bank will announce its next interest-rate decision on Thursday. At its last meeting in September, the South African Reserve Bank unanimously voted to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 7.25%, citing the energy price shock.
"The hurdle for another rate hike is likely to be high," Commerzbank analyst Volkmar Baur said in a note.
"For the SARB to act again this year, inflation would have to surprise significantly to the upside in the coming months."
Japan
Japan's third-quarter gross domestic product data on Monday will be watched for signs that the economy stalled, with some economists projecting the first contraction in four quarters.

A weak growth reading is unlikely to deter the Bank of Japan from further monetary tightening given persistent inflation, according to economists. Consumer price data due Friday are expected to show inflation accelerated in October.
A speech by hawkish BOJ board member Hajime Takata on Monday will also be closely watched for hints on the timing of the next interest-rate hike and his assessment of upside price risks.
Trade data for October and machinery orders figures for September are due Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
The Ministry of Finance is scheduled to auction 10-year inflation-linked bonds on Monday and 20-year government bonds on Wednesday.
The BOJ plans to conduct purchases of Japanese government bonds with maturities of three to five years, five to 10 years and longer than 25 years on Thursday.
China
China's October activity data on Monday will offer a fresh assessment of the economy, with industrial output, retail sales, housing prices and investment figures due.
Economists polled by The Wall Street Journal broadly expect continued weakness across gauges of fixed-asset investment, industrial production and retail sales.

Retail sales growth is expected to have eased to 0.9% on the year in October from 1.1% the prior month. Factory output growth is tipped to have cooled to 5.2% from 5.5%, while the contraction in fixed-asset investment is projected to have narrowed moderately to 7%.
Home price and property investment data are unlikely to show much improvement in the real-estate sector, according to economists.
Attention will turn Friday to the monthly loan prime rate announcement, with the benchmarks for most consumer and business lending widely expected to remain unchanged.

UOB economist Ho Woei Chen said that despite weak consumer inflation, the likelihood of a near-term policy rate cut is low following mortgage support measures and targeted credit easing. "Fiscal policy support will be the near-term focus to stabilize growth," Ho said.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' summit in Shenzhen will also be closely watched for developments in U.S.-China relations.

President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to meet on the sidelines of the summit, which would mark their third meeting this year. The talks would follow China's extension on Monday of the suspension of certain trade measures against the U.S. by two months.
Investors will also watch for confirmation of a possible trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the event.
Australia / New Zealand
Remarks from Reserve Bank of Australia Gov. Michele Bullock, policy meeting minutes and employment data will help investors assess the prospect of further interest-rate increases.
Markets are downplaying the risk of a sixth interest-rate rise in December or when the central bank's policy-setting board meets in February.

Bullock will speak at a conference on Tuesday, just ahead of the release of minutes from the bank's last policy meeting. Her remarks will be scrutinized for signs that persistent inflation and elevated capacity pressures could warrant another increase.

The minutes will offer further insight into how policymakers are weighing those pressures against signs of weakness in the economy. Recent data have shown a sharp drop in housing finance, while some economists predict this year's fall in house prices could be the biggest on record.
Consumer confidence at its lowest level in 50 years and any further decline in oil prices could strengthen the case for keeping rates on hold.

Thursday's employment data for October will provide another test of the outlook. A further rise in unemployment could temper expectations for another hike, though the central bank has continued to emphasize tightness in the labor market.
Indonesia
Bank Indonesia's interest-rate decision on Wednesday will be watched for signs of further tightening as policymakers prioritize rupiah stability.
The central bank is expected to keep its benchmark rate unchanged at 5.75% while maintaining a hawkish stance, ANZ economist Dhiraj Nim said.

Bank Indonesia has room to defend the currency through foreign-exchange intervention and other liquidity measures without raising its main policy rate, he said. However, renewed rupiah weakness or worsening external conditions could tilt the decision toward a hike, the economist added.
Malaysia
Malaysia's final third-quarter GDP figures on Wednesday will lead a busy data week, followed by October inflation on Thursday and exports on Friday.
The GDP reading is expected to confirm the preliminary growth estimate of 5.3%, ANZ's Sanjay Mathur said in a note.

Friday's trade figures could show exports rose 50% on year in October, supported by robust electrical and electronics shipments amid strong AI-related demand, DBS economists Taimur Baig and Chua Han Teng said in a note. Higher energy prices are also expected to have supported oil and gas exports.

Headline inflation could edge up to 2% in October from 1.8% in September, reflecting higher energy prices and a low base effect, although fuel subsidies continue to contain the pass-through to consumers, the DBS economists said.
South Korea

The Korea Development Institute's economic outlook on Wednesday will be watched for changes to its growth and inflation forecasts, as well as its assessment of how far the semiconductor boom is spreading through the economy.
In its previous outlook, published in August, the institute projected economic growth of 3.2% in 2026, supported by favorable conditions in the global semiconductor market, and 2.2% in 2027.

The new forecasts will also show whether its assessment of price pressures has shifted. In August, it projected headline inflation of 2.7% in 2026, reflecting higher international oil prices and improved economic conditions, before easing to 2.2% in 2027 as oil prices stabilize.
Singapore

Singapore's October trade figures on Tuesday are expected to show another strong month of electronics exports, offering an early indication of the economy's performance in the final quarter, according to economists.
The release will follow stronger-than-expected nonoil domestic export growth in September, when AI-related demand helped more than double electronics shipments on the year.
Another solid reading would bode well for the small economy, though investors will watch for signs that export momentum is easing.
Consensus estimates point to a slowdown in on-year NODX growth in October, with UOB economists predicting a 37.7% rise compared with September's 68.4% increase.
Thailand
Thailand's third-quarter GDP data on Monday are expected to show growth accelerated after a period of lackluster expansion.
Economists polled by The Wall Street Journal project growth of 3% on the year, which would mark the strongest reading since the first quarter of 2025.

The breakdown will be watched for the contribution from private investment. Goldman Sachs economists expect it to emerge as the main driver, supported by capital spending on data-center buildouts fueled by the AI boom.
"However, because this investment relies heavily on imported equipment, net exports will likely weigh on growth and partly offset the investment boost," Goldman Sachs said.
Any references to days are in local times.
